analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects about 1.07 million acres around the Grand Canyon from new mining and drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on July 12, 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create the Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni Grand Canyon National Monument on about 1,069,970 acres of federal land in northern Arizona and permanently bar new mining claims and mineral leasing on that land [S2]. It would give the twelve associated tribes a formal commission to help manage the monument and protect sacred sites [S2]. Hunting, fishing, existing grazing permits, existing water rights, and public access would all continue unchanged [S2]. The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: The Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, Navajo Nation, and the other tribes with ancestral ties to the Grand Canyon would gain a formal role in managing land that holds their sacred sites [S2]. Millions of Americans who drink Colorado River water would gain protection for the aquifers and springs that feed it, since the bill withdraws the land from new mining that could contaminate them [S2]. Hunters, hikers, campers, and the local towns that live off tourism would keep the existing uses the bill expressly preserves [S2]. Cattle ranchers with existing grazing permits would keep grazing under the same rules as before [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribes, recreation towns, and water drinkers

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a national monument on approximately 1,069,970 acres of public land and withdraws it from new mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, subject to valid existing rights [S2].

Creates a Tribal commission with one representative from each of the twelve associated tribes to guide the monument's management plan, and directs agencies to incorporate tribal knowledge and identify co-stewardship opportunities [S2].
Protects Indian sacred sites and tribal access for ceremonial, cultural, and traditional gathering purposes, including limited temporary closures for tribal religious activities [S2].
Expressly preserves hunting and fishing under state law, existing livestock grazing, existing water rights, and general public access, so everyday outdoor uses of the land are unchanged [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Uranium and other hardrock mining companies would lose the ability to stake new claims and lease minerals across the roughly 1.07 million acres, and holders of unpatented claims without valid existing rights would see their prospects end [S2]. Anyone who wants to develop motorized routes off the designated network, or mine sand and gravel beyond what the secretary permits, would face new limits [S2].

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal ends all new mineral and geothermal development on the land, which forecloses future domestic uranium and other mineral production from the area [S2]. Opponents in mining states generally argue such withdrawals lock up mineral resources the country may need, particularly uranium for nuclear fuel.

Motorized and mechanized vehicles would be allowed only on routes designated in the management plan, which would restrict off-road vehicle access beyond the exceptions for administrative, wildlife, emergency, and hunting-and-fishing use [S2].

The bill exempts the locations of cultural resources in the monument from Freedom of Information Act disclosure, reducing public transparency about what is on public land, though agencies may disclose when doing so poses no undue risk of harm or theft [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is carefully drafted: it withdraws the land from new mining while carving out everything people actually use today — grazing, hunting, fishing, water rights, roads, utilities, and access [S2]. The real cost falls on mining interests, mainly uranium claimholders, who lose access to over a million acres. The strongest honest objection is not that the land gets mismanaged but that a future need for the minerals is foreclosed; against that, the bill's own findings state that the watershed feeds the Colorado River, a drinking-water source for millions, and that recreation is the primary economic driver for local communities [S2]. As written, the protections outweigh the forgone mining.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on July 12, 2023 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill with Rep. Ruben Gallego as an original cosponsor, and two House Democrats cosponsored in total [S2][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on the day it was introduced [S1][S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S4].

In practice, the land got much of the same protection anyway: President Biden designated the Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni Grand Canyon National Monument by presidential proclamation in August 2023, which a later president could reverse, unlike the permanent statutory withdrawal this bill would have enacted (widely reported).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Uranium mining interests avoided a permanent, statute-level withdrawal of the land from mining. Tribes and conservation backers still received most of the protection they sought through the 2023 presidential proclamation, but that protection can be undone by a later president, which is what the failed bill would have prevented.

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited its cosponsors; it was referred to the Natural Resources Committee, where he served as the panel's senior Democrat.

for.name: Rep. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor on the day of introduction.

for.name: Associated Tribes of the Grand Canyon
for.role: Coalition of 12 tribes including the Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, and Navajo Nation
for.what_they_did: Led the multi-year campaign for permanent protection of the Grand Canyon watershed, including designation of the monument, after first seeking it through the 2023 presidential proclamation.

against.name: Bruce Westerman
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without any committee action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Uranium mining industry and claimholders near the Grand Canyon
against.role: Mining interests holding claims in the withdrawn area
against.what_they_did: Opposed permanent withdrawal of the Grand Canyon watershed from new mining, including litigation and lobbying against monument designation.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred. All three sponsors were Arizona Democrats, and the Republican-run Natural Resources Committee took no action on the bill [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill withdraws the full monument area from new mining claims and mineral and geothermal leasing, ending new extraction across roughly 1.07 million acres [S2]. Its interest runs against the public here because mining in the watershed risks the aquifers and springs that feed the Colorado River, a drinking-water source for millions [S2].

The bill keeps hunting, fishing, hiking, camping, and other recreation open and declares recreation the primary economic driver for local communities, so the tourism economy around the canyon is protected while the land that draws visitors is shielded from mining [S2].
Grazing established or permitted before enactment continues under existing law, so ranchers keep their use of the land while new mining is locked out [S2].
